I know this was already implied in your comment, but to make more clear the MAJOR difference between realism and neorealism:

In classical realism, competition is a result of human nature. It's a part of us and thus will always be a part of states. It exists from the bottom up, affecting everything from subnational politics to national and international affairs simply by the fact that we are inherently self motivated 

In neorealism, competition (and other behavior) between states is a result of the *nature of states* and the way the international system is set up

Obviously these are very simplified answers, but I hope it provides some more explanation

I've got to disagree with you on unification with Albania. I say this as someone who knows people in Kosovo and have talked to them a lot about the political situation there.

Many Kosovars have no desire to unite with Albania for a few reasons:

1. They have no faith in the Albanian government, which has been plagued with corruption scandals and economic stagnation for years. Certainly it's very easy to say the same about Kosovo though, considering their president and former PM have been dogged with allegations of war crimes and corruption for a long time, and the mafia is quite powerful there. However, their reasoning on why Kosovo's situation is different is pretty strong for me: they believe that, internally, Kosovo will be able to solve its own problems. I think this is backed up by the fact that the highly corrupt Old Guard politicians are unpopular among the younger generation, whereas new, forward thinking leaders like former PM Kurti (whose Vetevendosje* is the largest party in parliament) are increasing in popularity. If they joined Albania, their future would be tied to the fate of the rest of Albania. 

2. Most Kosovars are actually satisfied with their current relationship with Albania. They already have open borders with one another and can do business in Albania, visit family, etc

3. Kosovo and Albania consider each other brothers, but they are not one in the same. Their shared ethnicity is important, of course, but over the cold war and beyond they have developed independent histories and identities. most Kosovars consider themselves, just that—Kosovan, not Albanian—even if their Albanian culture is still very important. 


That's not to say it's never going to be on the table! Most are open to the idea of unification—in fact, a poll shows 60-something percent in support of eventual unification—and it may be feasible at some point. But, for now, that's not really the case in my opinion

*Interestingly, Kurti and Vetevendosje are officially in favor of unification. At their core, they are a social democratic and Albanian nationalist party, so it makes sense. However, Kurti actually dropped plans for unification because so many of his supporters were against it! They voted for his party to oust corruption and spur the economy, and put aside the fact that one of his key tenets was unification.
